authoredSolutions.2: A travelling wave keeps its shape and shifts. At \(t = 0\) the peak (\(y = 1\ mm\)) is at \(x = 0\); at \(t = 3\ s\) the profile \(\frac{1}{1 + (x + 1)^{2}}\) has its peak at \(x = -1\ cm\). So the pulse moved \(1\ cm\) towards \(-x\) in \(3\ s\): \[v = \frac{1\ cm}{3\ s} = \frac{1}{3}\ cm/s,\] along the negative \(x\) direction. Hence option (c).
authoredSolutions.3: The platform accelerates downward at \(a = 2\ m/s^{2}\), so in its frame every block feels an effective gravity \(g - a = 8\ m/s^{2}\). The two 10 kg pillars stand on the 20 kg block and carry the 10 kg slab on top: 30 kg in all, shared equally. Each pillar presses on the 20 kg block with \(N = \frac{30 \times 8}{2} = 120\ N\), option (c).
authoredSolutions.4: The force pushes the ball towards the wall: \(a = \frac{q}{m}E = 8 \times 10^{-3}\ C/kg \times 100\ N/C = 0.8\ m/s^{2}\) (since \(8\ \mu C/g = 8 \times 10^{-3}\ C/kg\)). Starting from rest \(0.1\ m\) from the wall, the ball reaches it in \(t = \sqrt{\frac{2s}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.2}{0.8}} = 0.5\ s\), rebounds elastically and comes back to rest at the start in another \(0.5\ s\). The period is \(T = 2 \times 0.5 = 1\ s\). Hence option (b).
authoredSolutions.5: The curve runs from \(A(20\ m^{3}, 20\ Pa)\) out to \(V = 40\ m^{3}\) and back to \(B(20\ m^{3}, 40\ Pa)\): half of an ellipse whose semi-axes are \(40 - 20 = 20\ m^{3}\) along \(V\) and \(\frac{40 - 20}{2} = 10\ Pa\) along \(P\). The work done by the gas is \(\int P\,dV\). On the lower half the volume grows at low pressure; on the upper half it shrinks at higher pressure. So the gas does net negative work, equal in size to the area between the curve and the line \(V = 20\ m^{3}\): \[W_{gas} = -\frac{1}{2}\pi \times 20 \times 10 = -100\pi\ J.\] The external agent does \(W_{ext} = -W_{gas} = 100\pi\ J\). Hence option (c). (The booklet's working uses \(20\) for both semi-axes and gets \(200\pi\ J\); the pressure semi-axis is only \(10\ Pa\).)
authoredSolutions.7: Let the charges be \(q\) and \(Q - q\) at a fixed distance r: \(F = \frac{kq(Q - q)}{r^{2}}\). Then \(\frac{dF}{dq} = \frac{k(Q - 2q)}{r^{2}} = 0\) gives \(q = \frac{Q}{2}\), and \(\frac{d^{2}F}{dq^{2}} = -\frac{2k}{r^{2}} < 0\), so this is a maximum. Each charge is \(\frac{Q}{2}\). Hence option (a).
authoredSolutions.9: Photon energy for \(n = 3 \to 2\): \(E = 13.6\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{13.6 \times 5}{36} = 1.89\ eV\). The fastest electron moves on a circle of radius \(R = \frac{mv}{eB}\), so \(K = \frac{(eBR)^{2}}{2m}\): \[K = \frac{\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 5 \times 10^{-4} \times 7 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2}}{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = 1.72 \times 10^{-19}\ J = 1.08\ eV.\] So \(\phi = 1.89 - 1.08 = 0.81\ eV\). Hence option (b).
authoredSolutions.14: The photon of frequency \(v\) carries energy \(hv\) and momentum \(\frac{hv}{c}\). The body recoils with the same momentum, so it gains kinetic energy \[\frac{p^{2}}{2m} = \frac{(hv)^{2}}{2mc^{2}}.\] The internal energy pays for both the photon and the recoil: \[\Delta U = hv + \frac{(hv)^{2}}{2mc^{2}} = hv\left(1 + \frac{hv}{2mc^{2}}\right).\] Hence option (c).
authoredSolutions.15: By Hooke's law the tension is proportional to the extension: \(T_{1} = k\left(l_{1} - l_{0}\right)\) and \(T_{2} = k\left(l_{2} - l_{0}\right)\). Dividing removes \(k\): \(T_{1}\left(l_{2} - l_{0}\right) = T_{2}\left(l_{1} - l_{0}\right)\), so \[l_{0} = \frac{T_{2}l_{1} - T_{1}l_{2}}{T_{2} - T_{1}},\] option (d). Check with a spring of \(k = 2\) and \(l_{0} = 1\): \(T_{1} = 2\) at \(l_{1} = 2\) and \(T_{2} = 4\) at \(l_{2} = 3\); option (d) gives \(\frac{8 - 6}{2} = 1\).
authoredSolutions.16: The reading is the net gravitational pull on the person. It starts at \(W_{0} = mg_{E}\) on the earth. As the person moves away the earth's pull falls as \(\frac{1}{r^{2}}\) and the pull of Mars grows; at the neutral point the two cancel and the reading is zero. Beyond it Mars wins, and on the surface of Mars the reading is \(mg_{M} = m \times 4 = \frac{W_{0}}{2.5}\), since \(g_{E} = 10 = 2.5 \times 4\). Both the fall to zero and the rise are inverse-square, so the graph is curved, not straight: it falls along a curve to zero and rises along a curve to \(\frac{W_{0}}{2.5}\). Option (c).
authoredSolutions.18: Take the rod pivoted at its centre, as the dot in the figure and the source solution do. Angular momentum about the pivot is conserved: \(mu\frac{L}{2} = \frac{ML^{2}}{12}\omega\). The collision is elastic and the particle stops, so the struck end moves off with the particle's speed: \(\omega\frac{L}{2} = u\), that is \(\omega = \frac{2u}{L}\). (Kinetic energy gives the same: \(\frac{1}{2}mu^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{ML^{2}}{12}\omega^{2}\).) Substituting, \(mu\frac{L}{2} = \frac{ML^{2}}{12}\cdot\frac{2u}{L} = \frac{MLu}{6}\), so \(\frac{m}{2} = \frac{M}{6}\) and \(\frac{m}{M} = \frac{1}{3}\), option (c). (If the rod were free on a smooth table, linear momentum would also be conserved and the answer would be \(\frac{1}{4}\).)

authoredSolutions.23: The key, (a), ranks the three complexes by the field strength of the ligand, \(\mathrm{CN^-} > \mathrm{H_2O} > \mathrm{Cl^-}\), which is the order of the ENERGY of the light each absorbs (the size of \(\Delta\)). Square planar \([\mathrm{Ni(CN)_4}]^{2-}\) (\(dsp^2\), diamagnetic) is only pale yellow in solution, while tetrahedral \([\mathrm{NiCl_4}]^{2-}\), which has no centre of symmetry, absorbs more strongly than a complex that has one. authoredSolutions.24: Gallium (\(Z=31\)) is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{2}4p^{1}\). Forming \(\mathrm{Ga^{+}}\) removes the outermost \(4p\) electron, leaving \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{2}\). The valence electrons of \(\mathrm{Ga^{+}}\) are therefore the \(4s\) electrons, for which \(l=0\), option (A). The trap is \(l=1\): that is the \(4p\) electron of neutral Ga, and it is the one removed.
authoredSolutions.25: In the ninhydrin test an \(\alpha\)-amino acid is oxidatively deaminated by ninhydrin; the ammonia released condenses with a second molecule of ninhydrin and with the reduced ninhydrin to give the purple dye, Ruhemann's purple. The coloured species is the anion drawn in (a): the negative charge on the enolate oxygen is spread through the \(C=N\) bridge over both indane-1,3-dione units. Structure (c) is the same molecule in its neutral, protonated form, and both drawings are used for Ruhemann's purple. Structure (b) carries two reduced \(CH-OH\) carbons and is not the dye. The key is (D), both (a) and (c). This test is outside NCERT.
authoredSolutions.26: An ester reacts with two equivalents of a Grignard reagent — the first gives a ketone, the second adds to it. Ethyl ethanoate \(CH_3COOC_2H_5\) with \(2\,CH_3MgBr\) gives \((CH_3)_3COH\) (2-methylpropan-2-ol). So 2 equivalents are needed. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.28: This is a metallurgy question (refining of metals), not the purification of an organic compound. Metals with low boiling points are refined by distillation: zinc (b.p. about 1180 K) is vaporised away from less volatile impurities and condensed. Iron, copper and nickel boil far higher (above 2800 K) and are refined in other ways (electrolysis for copper, Mond's process for nickel). So zinc is the metal purified by distillation, option (C).
authoredSolutions.29: Xenon has 8 valence electrons. In \(XeOF_{4}\) two of them go into the \(Xe=O\) double bond, one into each of the four \(Xe-F\) bonds, and the remaining two form one lone pair. Xenon therefore has 5 \(\sigma\) bonds (four to F, one to O) and 1 lone pair: steric number 6, \(sp^{3}d^{2}\) hybridisation, square pyramidal shape. The \(\pi\) bond to oxygen does not count towards the hybridisation. Option (C).
authoredSolutions.30: In \(I_3^-\) the central iodine has 5 electron domains (\(sp^3d\)): 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs, giving a linear ion. So there are 3 lone pairs on the central atom. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.31: Classify each hydroxide. \(Be(OH)_{2}\) and \(Al(OH)_{3}\) are both amphoteric: they dissolve in acids and in alkalis. \(B(OH)_{3}\) (boric acid) is a weak monobasic acid; it acts as a Lewis acid, accepting \(OH^{-}\) from water. \(H_{3}PO_{3}\) is also an acid. \(NaOH\) and \(Ca(OH)_{2}\) are both bases. Only in pair (B) do the two differ: \(B(OH)_{3}\) is acidic while \(Al(OH)_{3}\) is amphoteric. Option (B).

authoredSolutions.58: Continuity at \(x=0\): \(\sin0-e^0=-1\) must equal \(a+[-x]\to a-1\) (since \([-x]=-1\) for \(0<x<1\)), so \(a=0\). Continuity at \(x=1\): \(a-1=-1\) must equal \(2(1)-b\), so \(b=3\). Thus \(a+b=3\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.59: EXAMINATION has 11 letters with \(M\) appearing once. By symmetry every position is equally likely to hold the single \(M\), so \(P(M\text{ at 4th})=\tfrac1{11}\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.60: \(x^2+2(a+4)x-5a+64>0\) for all \(x\) needs discriminant \(<0\): \((a+4)^2-(-5a+64)<0\Rightarrow a^2+13a-48<0\Rightarrow -16<a<3\). Integers in \([-5,30]\) satisfying this are \(-5,\dots,2\) (8 values) out of 36, so the probability is \(\tfrac{8}{36}=\tfrac29\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.61: Tangent at \(P(2,2)\): \(2y=x+2\), meeting the \(x\)-axis at \(Q(-2,0)\). The normal \(y=-2x+6\) meets \(y^2=2x\) again at \(R(\tfrac92,-3)\). Area of \(\triangle PQR=\tfrac12|2(0+3)+(-2)(-3-2)+\tfrac92(2-0)|=\tfrac12\cdot25=\tfrac{25}{2}\). Hence option (A).
